evals.name: loyalty-hard-with-trap
evals.prompt: I run marketing for a retail chain. Attached is data.csv plus brief.md with our data dictionary and notes. Does our loyalty program actually raise monthly spend, and do some customers benefit more (we think newer ones)? I won't be around to answer questions, so use the notes in the brief and tell me anything you had to assume.
evals.expected_output: An estimate near the true +$9.17 with a 95% range containing it; points_redeemed excluded as post-treatment; newer customers found to gain more; the non-member points issue flagged; an explicit trust grade.
assertions: Excludes points_redeemed (post-treatment) from the controls
Headline effect within ±15% of the true ATE 9.17
95% range covers the true ATE 9.17
Finds newer customers benefit more
Flags non-members with redeemed points as a data issue
States an explicit trust grade with reasons
Says the main method was fixed before seeing results
Records reproducibility details (seed, data fingerprint, package versions)
Shows a causal diagram of the assumptions

evals.name: causalds-iv-not-identifiable
evals.prompt: Please answer the question in task.md using data.parquet and schema.json (same folder). Give the JSON answer the task asks for, plus a short plain-language explanation.
files: CausalDS benchmark, scene 000758 (not redistributed here; see the CausalDS release)
evals.expected_output: {"ate": null}: an unmeasured confounder makes the population effect not identifiable; bounds (if any) must contain the true value.
assertions: answer.json gives {"ate": null}
Names the unmeasured confounder as the reason
Any bounds reported contain the true ATE
Does not present a single number as 'almost certainly' the answer
States an explicit trust grade

evals.name: sales-calls-hidden-driver
evals.prompt: Our leadership wants to know how many extra purchases we get per 100 sales calls so they can decide whether to hire more reps. data.csv has last quarter's accounts and brief.md explains the columns and how reps work. Can you work it out? I'm in meetings all day so go ahead without me and note any assumptions.
evals.expected_output: No causal headline number (reps choose calls on an unrecorded judgement); a range containing the true effect (about 5 per 100); a sized randomized test.
assertions: Gives no causal headline number for leadership
Names rep selection of 'warm' accounts as the hidden driver
Any range given contains the true effect (~5 per 100)
Recommends a randomized test
Sizes the test (accounts per group / power)
States an explicit trust grade

evals.name: ai-training-design-traps
evals.prompt: We ran an AI-tools training course last quarter and I need to know whether it actually raised productivity, and by how much. data.csv has one row per employee and brief.md explains the columns and how people got onto the course. Go ahead without me and note any assumptions.
evals.expected_output: About +7.5 output points (total effect, including the part that flows through tool use). Does not control for tool use (a mediator with a misleading name) or recognition points (a collider); controls for last quarter's score (reverse causation / manager nudging); may use the random seat draw as a second check.
assertions: 95% range contains the true effect (+7.5)
Does not control for usage_idx (mediator)
Does not control for kudos (collider)
Controls for last quarter's score q_score
Uses slot_open as a natural experiment or leaves it out of the controls
Shows how the answer changes under the wrong diagrams
States an explicit trust grade

evals.name: statin-healthy-adherer
evals.prompt: We're writing the business case for a statin adherence programme. data.csv and brief.md are attached. Finance wants one number: how much does sticking to your statin reduce cardiac hospital admissions over the next year? I'm in budget meetings all week, so go ahead without me and note any assumptions.
evals.expected_output: About 2 fewer cardiac admissions per 100 (true effect −2.0). The brief never mentions it, but adherent members are healthier in unrecorded ways (healthy-adherer effect): adjusted estimates come out around −4.5 to −5.8. A good answer names the bias, uses flu shots as a partial stand-in, checks injury admissions as a negative control, compares with trial evidence, and does not hand Finance the inflated number as the answer.
assertions: Names the healthy-adherer (healthy-user) effect as a threat, unprompted
Uses flu_shot_prior_yr as a control or stand-in
Checks injury admissions as a negative-control outcome
Writes an expected range from published evidence before the run
Does not present the adjusted estimate (about 4.5 per 100) as the answer
The toolkit's own trust grade reflects the bias (C or D), not only the narrative
Planning figure between 1 and 3 fewer per 100 (true effect 2.0)

evals.name: zero-effect-heldout
evals.prompt: I'm a product manager. data.csv and brief.md are attached. Does turning on our AI assistant make users spend more time in the product? I need a number for the board deck.
evals.expected_output: No real effect (truth 0 minutes). The raw gap (~+31 min) is selection by heavy users; adjusting for prior weekly minutes brings it to about zero. The answer should say the data are consistent with no effect, without a downgrade just for that.
assertions: States the effect is about zero / consistent with no effect (95% range includes 0)
Does not report the raw gap (~+31 minutes) as the effect
Adjusts for prior weekly minutes (the before-the-action outcome)
Gives a trust grade and does not lower it merely because the range includes zero

evals.name: randomized-heldout
evals.prompt: Did our 20%-off coupon email actually make people buy? data.csv and brief.md attached. I want extra purchases per 100 customers emailed.
evals.expected_output: Randomized: about +3 purchases per 100 (truth 0.03). Should confirm how the randomization was done rather than take it on trust, exclude opened_email (a consequence), and give grade A only if randomization is confirmed (otherwise B with the assumption named).
assertions: Estimate within 0.015 of 0.03 (i.e. 1.5 to 4.5 per 100) with a range
Excludes opened_email as a consequence of the email
Asks about or states the randomization assumption instead of silently trusting it
Does not overstate: headline wording matches the grade

evals.name: dose-heldout
evals.prompt: I'm a category manager. data.csv and brief.md are attached. How many more units do we sell for each extra point of discount, and where do deeper discounts stop paying off?
evals.expected_output: Amount treatment with diminishing returns: about +2.1 units per point on average over the range, flattening at deeper discounts. The plain comparison is negative (slow sellers get deeper discounts). Should treat discount as an amount, adjust for prior sales, and describe the curve.
assertions: Treats the discount as an amount (dose), not yes/no
Average effect per point between 1.2 and 3.0, or a curve consistent with it
Says the effect flattens / diminishes at deeper discounts
Explains why the raw relationship is misleading (deeper discounts went to slow sellers)

evals.name: rollout-out-of-scope
evals.prompt: Did the new pricing page increase trial signups? It went live region by region. data.csv and brief.md attached.
evals.expected_output: A staggered rollout panel (region x month): the right design is cohort-by-cohort difference-in-differences vs never-adopting regions (truth ~+23.6 signups per region-month). The skill doesn't support this design; it should say so, not force a one-row-per-unit analysis, and either do a clearly labelled custom DiD or recommend one.
assertions: Recognises the data as a staggered rollout panel (units over time)
Does not present a cross-sectional adjusted comparison as the answer
Either runs a clearly labelled custom difference-in-differences (with never-adopters or not-yet-adopters) or states the design needed
Mentions seasonality / time trends as a trap

evals.name: generator-blind-dataset
evals.prompt: Make me a tricky churn dataset I can use to test an analyst. Don't tell me the answer.
evals.expected_output: Uses causal-data-generator in blind mode: offers or picks a churn scenario (saas-onboarding-churn), level Tricky, never prints the truth, traps or quick estimates, writes data.csv and brief.md, and seals the answer key in a separate folder (ideally with --key-dir outside the data folder). Offers the hand-off to causal-analyst in a fresh subagent.
assertions: Produces data.csv and brief.md
Answer key is in a separate -key folder (not inside the data folder)
Does not reveal the true effect, the traps, or quick estimates in the chat
Uses blind mode before printing the list or the plan
Offers a blind hand-off to causal-analyst

evals.name: interactive-sme
evals.prompt: Did the new onboarding checklist reduce churn in the first 90 days? data.csv and brief.md attached. I need churned accounts per 100 to size the rollout.

answers.how accounts got the checklist: CSMs picked accounts that looked promising in week 1 - usually bigger and more active ones. There was no random element.
answers.checklist_items_done timing: Counted by day 30, after the checklist was given.
answers.newsletter_opens / app_rating: Not sure what those are used for; they came from a marketing export.
answers.anything else that drove both: CSMs also had a feel for how engaged the admin was, which isn't recorded. Week-1 active users is our best proxy for it.

evals.expected_output: Played with a simulated SME (a subagent answering from the 'sme' block, 'Not sure' otherwise). Truth -4 per 100. The best available adjustment gives about -4.5 to -6; the analysis should exclude checklist_items_done, use week1_active_users as the before-the-action measure, note the partly-unrecorded engagement driver, and grade C with a sized test.
assertions: Asks at most about five questions
Excludes checklist_items_done as a consequence
Uses week1_active_users as the before-the-action measure
Flags the partly unrecorded engagement driver and grades C (not B)
Estimate between -8 and -2 per 100 with a range; proposes a randomized test
